sections.h2: Who collects property tax in Williamson County, and who values the house?
sections.html:
The Trustee collects, the Property Assessor values, and elected bodies set the rates. Karen Paris is the Trustee, at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 203, Franklin, TN 37064, phone 615-790-5709, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 to 4:30. The Assessor's office takes valuation and mailing-address questions at 615-790-5708.

The county's rate page states that the Assessor does not set rates, send bills or collect taxes. The Trustee uses the rate and the Assessor's roll to produce the bills. The Trustee's page names what the office collects for: Williamson County, the Franklin Special School District, Brentwood, Franklin, Nolensville and Thompson's Station. For Spring Hill and Fairview the county's rate page says to contact the city, so a buyer or seller in those two should ask city hall which office bills.

Under Tennessee law the Trustee has no power to waive, prorate or release tax or interest (T.C.A. 67-5-2803). A request to forgive a penalty will not succeed at the counter.

sections.h2: What is Williamson County like, and why are values here so high?
sections.html:
Williamson County is in Middle Tennessee, south of Nashville, with Franklin as the county seat. The General Assembly created it on October 26, 1799 from part of Davidson County. Abram Maury laid out Franklin in 1800. The county covers about 584 square miles, and the Harpeth River and Little Harpeth River are its main streams. The Natchez Trace Parkway crosses it.

History is part of the housing stock. The Battle of Franklin was one of the war's deadliest, and the McGavock Confederate Cemetery holds 1,481 soldiers. The Dortch Stove works factory in Franklin was later reused for offices, restaurants and event space. Growth since the interstates arrived has been fast: the 2020 census counted 247,726 people, a 35.2 percent jump from 2010, the largest gain in the county's history. The south end is still mostly rural, while Brentwood and Franklin anchor the north. Schools are run by Williamson County Schools, with a part of Franklin served by the Franklin Special School District for grades K through 8.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Williamson County:

  • 272,061 residents in July 2025, up 9.8% from the April 2020 base
  • 103,674 housing units, with 78.8% owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied home value of $751,900, against $249,000 in Washington County and $240,600 in Tipton County
  • Median household income of $135,594, and 62.7% of adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or higher
  • 1,621 building permits in 2025

sections.h2: How is Williamson County property tax figured?
sections.html:
Tennessee assessment ratios apply: residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, commercial and industrial at 40 percent, and business personal property at 30 percent. The bill is the assessed value times the rate for each $100. At a $751,900 home, the Census median, the assessed value would be $187,975, so every $1.00 of rate per $100 would add about $1,880 to the bill.

The county posts its 2026 rates as a chart on its Property Tax Rates page, and the county rate has to be combined with the city or school district that applies to the address. Brentwood, Franklin, Nolensville, Thompson's Station and the Franklin Special School District are billed through the Trustee. The Assessor values new construction up to September 1, and then the rolls pass to the Trustee.

The roll is open to the public in May, and owners whose value changed get a notice by mail. The county's Board of Equalization has five members, each appointed by the County Commission to a two-year term. Reading the roll early lets an owner act before the June hearing window.

sections.h2: When is Williamson County property tax due?
sections.html:
Bills go out in early October. Tax is due from the first Monday in October through February 28 of the next year, and partial payments are accepted. Interest of 1.5 percent is added on March 1 and keeps accruing at the start of each month. The tax year runs January 1 through December 31. Today is November 15, 2026, so the 2026 bill is payable and no interest has started.

A homeowner whose lender pays the tax still gets the statement, which the Trustee says is for the owner's records. Ask the Trustee's office which payment methods it takes for the 2026 bill.

Two rules from the Trustee's FAQ come up often:

  • The bill goes to the owner of record on January 1, and a seller who has already sold must forward it to the new owner
  • Interest cannot be waived, because the Trustee has no authority to do so

sections.h2: How does a Williamson County owner appeal a valuation?
sections.html:
Call the Assessor at 615-790-5708 to review the value, and also protect the appeal rights. The county's page says many disagreements settle at this level, yet the owner still has to make the appointment with the County Board of Equalization on time. The board meets in June, and the Assessor's office asks owners to call during the first week of June to be placed on the schedule. Only the person named on the roll, an authorized agent or the property owner can file.

A taxpayer not satisfied at the county level can go to the State Board of Equalization. The state sets the deadline at August 1 of the tax year or 45 days after the county board's notice, whichever is later, and a ruling from the administrative judge follows within 90 days of the hearing. The state calls sales of comparable properties the best evidence of value for a house, and a bare claim that the value is too high is generally not enough. Pay the undisputed part of the bill before it turns delinquent.

sections.h2: What tax relief and freeze programs does Williamson County offer?
sections.html:
The Trustee administers four programs, two of them state-funded, and appointments are required. Disabled veterans and their widows or widowers have a separate state program, so call for the paperwork it needs. All take 2025 income from every source for the applicant, spouse and co-owners, and the elderly ones need the applicant to be 65 by December 31, 2026. The brochure for tax year 2026 lists these income limits:

ProgramCombined 2025 income limitSource
State relief, elderly or disabled$38,470Williamson County Tax Relief Brochure TY 2026
County Broad Base relief, elderly$63,000Williamson County Tax Relief Brochure TY 2026
County Tax Freeze, age 65 or older$69,150Williamson County Tax Relief Brochure TY 2026

Applications for 2026 relief are taken after the 2026 bill arrives and until April 5, 2027, with the tax paid in full first. The freeze fixes the home's tax at the qualifying year's amount for as long as the owner re-qualifies every year. It covers the residence and up to 5 acres, and the base resets if improvements raise the value or the owner buys another home. Call 615-790-5709 to book.

sections.h2: What happens to property tax when a Williamson County house sells?
sections.html: The January 1 owner is billed, so the seller gets the notice even after a fall closing and is responsible for forwarding it to the buyer. Ask the title company how the 2026 tax will be split in the settlement statement. A seller who is in a freeze program should ask the Trustee before closing, since selling and buying another residence changes the base amount for the next home.

faqs.q: Where is the Williamson County Trustee's office?
faqs.a: It is at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 203, in Franklin, open weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30. The phone number is 615-790-5709.

faqs.q: When are Williamson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due from the first Monday in October through February 28. Interest of 1.5 percent starts March 1.

faqs.q: Can Williamson County waive property tax interest?
faqs.a: No. The Trustee states that it has no authority to waive, prorate or release any part of the tax or the interest.

faqs.q: What is the income limit for the Williamson County tax freeze?
faqs.a: For tax year 2026 the combined 2025 income of the applicant, spouse and co-owners cannot exceed $69,150, and the applicant must be 65 by December 31, 2026.

faqs.q: Who do I call to question my Williamson County assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Property Assessor at 615-790-5708. For an appeal, ask for the County Board of Equalization appointment during the first week of June.
